## Objectives

By the end of today you will be able to:

1. Create a data frame from vectors.
2. Inspect a data frame with `str()`, `head()`, `summary()`, `nrow()` and `ncol()`.
3. Pick out columns with `$` and `[ ]`.
4. Pick out rows by position and by a condition.
5. Add a new column.
6. Create a list and get values out of it.

## Data frames: tables in R

A **data frame** is a table. Each column is a vector, and all the columns have the same length. Each row is one observation, such as one person, one household or one day.

```{webr}
households <- data.frame(
  id        = c(101, 102, 103, 104, 105),
  district  = c("Gulu", "Arua", "Gulu", "Mbale", "Arua"),
  size      = c(4, 6, 2, 7, 5),
  has_water = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)
households
```

Each column has its own type. `district` is character, `size` is numeric and `has_water` is logical.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Excel bridge
A data frame is like an Excel sheet with headers in row 1 and one record per row. The difference: in R, every value in a column must have the same type. You cannot have a number in one cell and a note in the next.
:::

## Inspecting a data frame

Real data is too large to read on screen, so you inspect it with functions. Today you will use the `penguins` data from the **palmerpenguins** package: measurements of 344 penguins on three islands in Antarctica.

```{webr}
library(palmerpenguins)
head(penguins)        # the first 6 rows
```

```{webr}
nrow(penguins)        # number of rows
ncol(penguins)        # number of columns
names(penguins)       # column names
```

`str()` ("structure") is the most useful one. It shows each column's name, type and first few values:

```{webr}
str(penguins)
```

`summary()` gives a quick summary of every column, including the number of missing values:

```{webr}
summary(penguins)
```

You may notice that `penguins` prints as a **tibble**. A tibble is a modern data frame. Everything you learn today works the same way on both.

## Picking columns

Use `$` and the column name to get one column as a vector:

```{webr}
penguins$island[1:10]
mean(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Use square brackets with two positions, `[rows, columns]`. Leave a position empty to mean "all":

```{webr}
households[, "size"]                 # one column, as a vector
households[, c("district", "size")]  # two columns, as a data frame
```

## Picking rows

```{webr}
households[2, ]          # the second row
households[1:3, ]        # the first three rows
```

The most useful way is by a condition, exactly as with vectors on Day 3. Put the condition in the rows position:

```{webr}
households[households$size > 4, ]
households[households$district == "Gulu", ]
households[households$has_water & households$size >= 4, ]
```

Notice the comma at the end. It means "all columns".

## Adding a column

Assign to a new column name with `$`:

```{webr}
households$size_group <- ifelse(households$size >= 5, "large", "small")
households
```

`ifelse()` checks a condition for every row and returns the first value where it is `TRUE` and the second where it is `FALSE`. You will learn more about it on Day 9.

## Counting categories

`table()` counts how often each value appears. It is the quickest way to summarise a category column:

```{webr}
table(penguins$species)
table(penguins$species, penguins$island)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Excel bridge
`table()` with two columns does the same job as a simple pivot table that counts rows.
:::

## Lists: containers for anything

A **list** can hold values of different types and lengths, including other lists and whole data frames. Many R functions return their results as lists.

```{webr}
survey <- list(
  name      = "Settlement survey 2026",
  districts = c("Gulu", "Arua", "Mbale"),
  n         = 1500,
  data      = households
)
str(survey, max.level = 1)
```

Get one item out of a list with `$` or with double brackets `[[ ]]`:

```{webr}
survey$districts
survey[["n"]]
```

Single brackets `[ ]` return a smaller list, not the item itself. This difference catches everyone out at first:

```{webr}
class(survey["n"])     # a list containing n
class(survey[["n"]])   # n itself
```

A data frame is a special kind of list: a list of columns of the same length. That is why `$` works on both.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1: Create a data frame

Create a data frame called `crops` with two columns:

- `crop`: `"maize"`, `"beans"`, `"cassava"`
- `tonnes`: `120`, `45`, `210`

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4_create
crops <- data.frame(
  crop   = ______,
  tonnes = ______
)
crops
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex4_create"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Each column is a vector made with `c()`. Text values need quotes.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex4_create"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
crops <- data.frame(
  crop   = c("maize", "beans", "cassava"),
  tonnes = c(120, 45, 210)
)
crops
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4_create
#| check: true
if (!exists("crops") || !is.data.frame(crops)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Create a data frame called crops with data.frame().")
} else if (!identical(names(crops), c("crop", "tonnes"))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The columns should be called crop and tonnes.")
} else if (!identical(crops$crop, c("maize", "beans", "cassava")) || !isTRUE(all.equal(crops$tonnes, c(120, 45, 210)))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The column names are right. Check the values.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. You built a data frame from two vectors.")
}
```

### Exercise 2: Inspect the data

How many penguins (rows) are in the `penguins` data frame?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4_nrow
#| setup: true
library(palmerpenguins)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4_nrow
______(penguins)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex4_nrow"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
One function counts rows and another counts columns. Their names start with `n`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex4_nrow"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
nrow(penguins)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4_nrow
#| check: true
if (identical(as.integer(.result), 344L)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: 344 penguins.")
} else if (identical(as.integer(.result), 8L)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the number of columns. Use nrow() for rows.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use nrow() on penguins.")
}
```

### Exercise 3: Summarise a column

What is the average flipper length (`flipper_length_mm`) of all the penguins? Some values are missing.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4_mean
#| setup: true
library(palmerpenguins)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4_mean
mean(______, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex4_mean"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Get the column with `penguins$` followed by the column name.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex4_mean"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
mean(penguins$flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4_mean
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, mean(penguins$flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct: about %.1f mm.", .result))
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use mean() on penguins$flipper_length_mm.")
}
```

### Exercise 4: Filter rows

Keep only the rows of `households` where the household does **not** have water. Save them as `no_water`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4_filter
#| setup: true
households <- data.frame(
  id        = c(101, 102, 103, 104, 105),
  district  = c("Gulu", "Arua", "Gulu", "Mbale", "Arua"),
  size      = c(4, 6, 2, 7, 5),
  has_water = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4_filter
no_water <- households[______, ]
no_water
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex4_filter"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
`has_water` is already `TRUE` or `FALSE`. The `!` symbol means "not": `!TRUE` is `FALSE`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex4_filter"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
no_water <- households[!households$has_water, ]
no_water
```
`households[households$has_water == FALSE, ]` also works.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4_filter
#| check: true
if (!exists("no_water")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Save the result as no_water.")
} else if (!is.data.frame(no_water)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "no_water should be a data frame. Keep the comma before ].")
} else if (identical(no_water$id, c(102, 105))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: households 102 and 105.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You should get households 102 and 105.")
}
```

### Exercise 5: Get an item from a list

Get the vector of districts out of the list `survey`, so that the result is a character vector, not a list.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4_list
#| setup: true
survey <- list(name = "Settlement survey 2026", districts = c("Gulu", "Arua", "Mbale"), n = 1500)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4_list
______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex4_list"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Use `$` or double brackets `[[ ]]` with the item name `districts`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex4_list"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
survey$districts
```
`survey[["districts"]]` gives the same result.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4_list
#| check: true
if (identical(.result, c("Gulu", "Arua", "Mbale"))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct.")
} else if (is.list(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You got a list back. Use [[ ]] or $ instead of [ ].")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use survey$districts.")
}
```

## Common mistakes

- **Forgetting the comma.** `households[households$size > 4]` without a comma tries to pick columns, not rows. Write `households[households$size > 4, ]`.
- **Forgetting the data frame name in a condition.** `households[size > 4, ]` fails, because `size` on its own does not exist. Write `households$size`.
- **Single brackets on a list.** `survey["n"]` is still a list. Use `survey[["n"]]` or `survey$n`.
- **Misspelt column names.** `penguins$bodymass` returns `NULL` without an error. Check the names with `names()`.

## Summary

- A data frame is a table of columns (vectors) of the same length. Create one with `data.frame()`.
- Inspect it with `head()`, `str()`, `summary()`, `nrow()`, `ncol()` and `names()`.
- `df$col` gives one column. `df[rows, columns]` picks rows and columns. Leave a position empty for "all".
- Filter rows with a condition: `df[df$col > 5, ]`.
- Add a column with `df$new <- ...`.
- `table()` counts categories.
- A list holds items of any type. Use `$` or `[[ ]]` to get an item out.
